newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Honecker's rifle-maker has future in its sights.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Honecker's rifle-maker has future in its sights.

text.p: When Erich Honecker capped a holiday in August 1989 by shooting a deer on a hunting trip, the chances are he had his finger on the trigger of a rifle made in the town of Suhl.

A few months later, the East German leader was out of a job and the prestigious company which made hunting weapons for members of the eastern bloc elite, including former Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev, nearly followed him into oblivion.
But now Suhler Jagd und Sportwaffen GmbH is looking forward to a future in a new factory on the outskirts of the southeastern town which has always been its home.

"We've been going for nearly 500 years, through various social and political forms, from feudalism and early capitalism," personnel manager Hartmut Weiss said. "And we've survived it all -- including East Germany."
The firm, a combination of several small companies amalgamated and nationalised by the communist authorities after World War Two, employed 2,000 people in its heyday.
"People knew they were doing something special and took particular pride in their jobs," recalled Rolf Scheermesser, who monitored productivity at the factory for more than 20 years.
HUNTING FOR HARD CURRENCY
The company's purpose was much more than just to provide new toys for Honecker and his hunting cronies.
As one of the few "People's Own Businesses" making specialist products which were in demand abroad, it brought in vital western currency to keep the whole system afloat.
"We were one of the largest suppliers of hard currency and the leadership recognised that," said Scheermesser, who retired from the company in 1989.
Around 85 percent of the firm's output, bearing renowned pre-communist brand names such as Simson and Merkel, was sold in the "non-socialist economies" of the West.
"One advantage for the firm today is that we always had to maintain our position in the international market," Weiss said.
One big disadvantage was that the company belonged to a bigger conglomerate from 1969, which siphoned off its profits instead of reinvesting them in the business.
After the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989, the company found itself in the same position as thousands of others across eastern Germany -- in the hands of the government's Treuhand agency.
The agency's job was to privatise as many businesses as possible, scouring the world for potential buyers.
It found one for the Suhl factory in shape of a partnership between French investment group Cie de Suez and Janivo Holdings of the Netherlands.
DEATH AND REBIRTH
The new owners took control in August 1992, promising to keep on 400 of the 2,000-strong workforce.
"Within three quarters of a year, we were bankrupt," Weiss recalled.
He is reluctant to discuss what went wrong but places a lot of the blame at the door of the Treuhand, saying they should have looked more closely at potential buyers.

"We always said the important preconditions for any potential buyer were that it could identify with the products, the workers, the company and with the location," he said. "Those criteria should have been observed."
Fortunately for the Suhl works, and in contrast to so many other tales of eastern German companies perishing in the chill winds of capitalism, this was not the end of the story.
Underscoring their determination to preserve a tradition of weapon manufacture in Suhl dating back to 1535, the workers occupied the plant in July 1993.
The receivers, meanwhile, began a new hunt for potential buyers, opting to try to sell the company as a going concern rather than simply wind it up as quickly as possible.
"We had stories of everyone from a Japanese bank to a Saudi prince being interested," Weiss said.
NEW BEGINNING
The eventual buyer was closer to home. In December 1993, Austria's Steyr-Mannlicher AG -- a unit of Steyr-Daimler-Puch AG -- acquired a majority stake.
Now the company employs around 160 people and has sales of around 10 million marks ($6.5 million). It's not in the black yet but aims to break even by the end of next year.

The move away from the traditional factory site, complete with timber framed buildings and sloped roofs, in the centre of Suhl provokes sadness among many in the town, for whom it has been a permanent fixture since childhood.
But most recognise the firm cannot just rely on its great tradition if it wants to survive in the market economy.
The machinery has already moved to the new site a few km (miles) from the town centre, and Weiss and his fellow top managers will join them by the end of the year.
"This location has a lot of tradition and atmosphere but costs play a big role," Weiss said. "You can't really be efficiently organised here."
